newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia daily raps U.S drug certification process.
newsitem.headline: Colombia daily raps U.S drug certification process.

text.p: A leading Colombian daily lashed out at the U.S. drug "certification" process on Monday, saying the United States has done too little to fight drugs in its own backyard to fairly judge another country.

In its lead editorial, Bogota's El Espectador predicted that U.S. President Bill Clinton would "decertify" Colombia for a second consecutive year because of its alleged failure to crack down hard enough on the drug trade.

But it said the decision, which the "imperial" U.S. president is to announce on Thursday of next week, would be prompted more by the Clinton administration's dislike of President Ernesto Samper than by objective facts.
In testimony last week on Capitol Hill, U.S. Assistant Secretary of State Robert Gelbard called Samper "a truly corrupt president who has had a clear history of cooperating with drug dealers."
El Espectador, which is no friend of Samper, has urged him to step down repeatedly because of his alleged ties to the drug lords who contributed up to $6 million to his 1994 election campaign.
But it stressed that too many Colombians have suffered on the front-lines of the drug war, and died in acts of "heroism and martyrdom," for anyone to claim that the country is "soft" on drugs.

"The (Colombian) police forces, intelligence services and justice system ... have achieved a great deal more against producers than U.S. authorities have achieved against the mafias or distributors there in their own territory," the newspaper said.
It added that the enormous U.S. appetite for illegal drugs was the root cause of the drug war and said that if anyone should be "decertified" it was the United States itself.

"If an impartial and objective international organization were to issue certificates about the two faces of the drug war, consumption as well as production, there can be little doubt about what would happen to a country whose demand stimulates production and (drug) shipments to its beaches and airports," El Espectador said.
